originalGroup.material:
The Box Made from the Same Metal

In a college science demonstration, a small solid metal piece sank in water while a larger closed metal box floated. Some students first explained the difference by saying that heavier objects sank. The tutor placed both objects on a scale. The floating box was heavier than the piece that had sunk.

The class then considered the space each object occupied. The box enclosed air as well as metal. Its total mass was spread over a much larger external volume, making its average density different from that of the solid piece. The material’s name alone did not determine the behaviour of the whole object.

As an object enters water, it displaces some water and experiences an upward force. For the closed box, enough water could be displaced to balance its weight before the whole box went below the surface. The smaller solid piece did not achieve that balance under the demonstration’s conditions.

The tutor did not claim that the shape had removed mass or changed the metal into a different substance. It changed the relationship between mass, enclosed space and displaced water. The box’s closure also mattered. If water entered and replaced the enclosed air, the behaviour could change. The class therefore recorded whether an example was closed or open, rather than place all metal containers in one category.

One student compared the box with a ship. The tutor accepted the comparison as a starting model, while noting that a real vessel involved structure, loading and operating conditions beyond the simple demonstration. The small box explained why weight alone was insufficient; it did not certify any boat’s suitability.

In their report, students included the masses, external shapes and conditions. They replaced the rule heavy things sink with an explanation that could account for the two observations together. An apparent exception had helped reveal what the first rule had left out.

Why the Paint Did Not Match the Screen

For a college exhibition, two students tried to copy a bright colour shown on a laptop. They mixed paints that seemed related to the colours used by the screen, but the result looked duller. One student thought the paint must be faulty. Their art tutor asked them to consider how the two displays produced visible light.

A screen sends light towards the viewer. Combining its light sources can add to the light reaching the eye. A painted surface usually depends on illumination falling upon it and on the light the pigments reflect. Mixing pigments can remove parts of that reflected light rather than behave like adding the screen’s light sources. The same everyday word mixing covered different processes.

The tutor placed the painted sample under two lamps. It did not look exactly the same in both places. The pigments had not been replaced; the available illumination had changed. A screen’s brightness and settings also affected the comparison. A colour match was a relationship under viewing conditions, not merely a recipe printed beside a pot.

The students kept physical samples and wrote down the conditions under which each had been judged. They stopped adjusting the paint solely to match a very bright screen in a dark room. Instead, they compared it in the gallery lighting where visitors would see the work.

The final paint was chosen for that setting. It was not described as an exact match under every possible lamp or device. The tutor also avoided claiming that all paints behaved identically, since pigment mixtures and surfaces could differ. What the students gained was a better question. They no longer asked only which two colour names to combine, but which light would reach a viewer through which materials in the place where the result would be used.

The Character Who Told the Story

In a writing class, Mira read a short story told by a character who believed his neighbour had taken a missing letter. He described a conversation through the wall and an empty place on his desk. Halfway through the story, a scene revealed to the reader that the neighbour was searching for her own lost key. The narrator did not see that scene.

A student objected that the story was inconsistent. The tutor asked which statements belonged to the narrator’s belief and which events the text showed more directly. The narrator had heard a conversation, but his explanation of it was not the only possible one. The story could show that his conclusion was mistaken without claiming that the conversation had never happened.

Mira then rewrote one passage from the neighbour’s point of view. The same knock at the door became a request for help with a key rather than evidence of guilt. This did not change the physical sound. It changed what information the reader had and the purpose assigned to the action.

The class also compared a version that disclosed the key immediately with one that delayed it. A Tree Is Not a Ladder

An evolutionary tree can be misread as a ladder with modern species arranged from less to more advanced. The visual order of the tips encourages this when one species is placed at the top of a page or the end of a row. Yet moving a branch around its point of connection can change that order without changing the relationships represented. Position on the page is not, by itself, a ranking of evolutionary achievement.

Consider an illustrative tree in which two living species share a more recent common ancestor with each other than either shares with a third. Neither of the two is therefore the living ancestor of the other. Both lineages have continued since their separation. A familiar species used as a comparison can help identify relationships without being treated as a specimen of the past that stopped changing while another lineage progressed.

Branch lengths require their own explanation. Some diagrams represent an estimated amount of change, some a time scale and some show only the branching pattern. Measuring a printed line with a ruler is meaningful only if the diagram’s convention supports that interpretation. A visually long branch does not automatically mean an old species, and a tidy equal spacing can be a design choice rather than a biological observation.

The relationships themselves are hypotheses supported by evidence and methods. Different genes or kinds of observation can present complications, and uncertainty may remain in particular connections. A simple drawing often omits that complexity to make one point legible. Its usefulness does not justify treating every visible junction as equally secure or every omitted uncertainty as resolved.

For a fictional teaching display, curators therefore rotated an example tree, showed that the relationships were unchanged and added a note about branch lengths. They asked visitors to identify common connections rather than choose which species was highest. The exercise did not require giving up a useful visual model. It required learning which features of the image carried the argument.

Uncertainty also needed a way to be shown. The team marked a disputed connection and explained that resolving it required evidence, rather than simply redrawing the tips in a more persuasive order.

The result was a more careful way of reading. A diagram could make shared history easier to inspect while remaining a representation with specified conventions. The tree’s explanatory power came from those relationships, not from a story of inevitable ascent hidden in the direction a page happened to face.

A Sale That Had Not Yet Happened

A fictional independent bookshop accepted a local publisher’s books on consignment. The books occupied shelf space and were offered to customers, but the shop had not bought the entire delivery outright. Under the agreement, payment to the publisher depended on recorded sales, with stated arrangements for unsold stock. Counting every delivered copy as an immediate completed sale would misdescribe the transaction.

The arrangement divided risk differently from an outright purchase. The publisher retained an interest in stock that had not yet sold, while the shop provided space, attention and selling work. This did not make consignment costless for either side. Time spent displaying a slow-selling title could displace another use of the shelf, and the publisher still needed a dependable record of what had happened to the copies.

The partners therefore distinguished stock received, stock currently held, customer sales, returns and copies damaged under the agreement. A low shelf count alone did not identify revenue: a copy might be waiting behind the counter or have been returned. The financial account followed the defined events rather than the appearance of a nearly empty display.

Price and settlement dates were stated too. A discount offered to customers could affect what each party received under the terms, so neither assumed the cover price was automatically the final amount owed for every copy. The publisher’s catalogue was not a substitute for the actual sales record.

At the review meeting, strong sales were welcomed, but the partners also considered whether the display served their purposes. A specialist title could matter to a small readership without becoming the shop’s fastest-moving book. They kept financial facts distinct from the judgement about what to carry.

At a stock check, both sides compared delivered copies with sales, returns, damaged copies and those still held. A discrepancy was a question to investigate, not proof of dishonesty. A memory that the display had looked full could not replace this record. Reconstructing actual movements helped identify what remained unexplained before either partner assigned responsibility.

The system worked through clear responsibilities and inspection rights, not simply through the friendly relationship that had begun it. The shop could host books without yet purchasing them all, the publisher could retain risk while gaining access to readers, and both could examine the events connecting stock to money. Naming that structure made an apparently ordinary shelf easier to understand as a set of continuing obligations.

questions.prompt: What makes the consignment different from the outright purchase described?
questions.material:
A Sale That Had Not Yet Happened

A fictional independent bookshop accepted a local publisher’s books on consignment. The books occupied shelf space and were offered to customers, but the shop had not bought the entire delivery outright. Under the agreement, payment to the publisher depended on recorded sales, with stated arrangements for unsold stock. Counting every delivered copy as an immediate completed sale would misdescribe the transaction.

The arrangement divided risk differently from an outright purchase. The publisher retained an interest in stock that had not yet sold, while the shop provided space, attention and selling work. This did not make consignment costless for either side. Time spent displaying a slow-selling title could displace another use of the shelf, and the publisher still needed a dependable record of what had happened to the copies.

The partners therefore distinguished stock received, stock currently held, customer sales, returns and copies damaged under the agreement. A low shelf count alone did not identify revenue: a copy might be waiting behind the counter or have been returned. The financial account followed the defined events rather than the appearance of a nearly empty display.

Price and settlement dates were stated too. A discount offered to customers could affect what each party received under the terms, so neither assumed the cover price was automatically the final amount owed for every copy. The publisher’s catalogue was not a substitute for the actual sales record.

At the review meeting, strong sales were welcomed, but the partners also considered whether the display served their purposes. A specialist title could matter to a small readership without becoming the shop’s fastest-moving book. They kept financial facts distinct from the judgement about what to carry.

At a stock check, both sides compared delivered copies with sales, returns, damaged copies and those still held. A discrepancy was a question to investigate, not proof of dishonesty. A memory that the display had looked full could not replace this record. Reconstructing actual movements helped identify what remained unexplained before either partner assigned responsibility.

The system worked through clear responsibilities and inspection rights, not simply through the friendly relationship that had begun it. The shop could host books without yet purchasing them all, the publisher could retain risk while gaining access to readers, and both could examine the events connecting stock to money. Naming that structure made an apparently ordinary shelf easier to understand as a set of continuing obligations.

originalGroup.material:
One Reference Is Not Every Good Answer

A fictional evaluation project compared generated summaries with a reference written by an editor. The reference was useful because it gave the team a concrete example of the desired content. Trouble began when similarity to its wording was treated as the complete definition of quality. A different summary could express the same supported information, while a closely matching one could repeat an error already present in the reference.

The team separated several questions: whether the summary contained required facts, whether its claims were supported by the source and whether it communicated them clearly. These dimensions could interact without being interchangeable. A fluent sentence might be unsupported, and an accurate list might omit a relationship essential to the task. A single overlap score could not establish all of them merely because it was easy to calculate consistently.

More references could widen the examples of acceptable expression. They would not automatically cover every valid answer or remove a shared misunderstanding. If all reference writers followed the same incomplete brief, agreement could preserve the same omission. The project recorded how references had been produced and checked them against the source material.

Human judgements also needed a stated task and procedure. Reviewers sometimes disagreed because one prioritised brevity while another expected additional context. Clarifying the intended use helped interpret that disagreement. Agreement after discussion was useful evidence about the adopted criteria, not proof that the criteria were the only possible ones for every summary a user might request.

The final report kept case examples alongside aggregate scores. It showed where the system omitted a fact, introduced an unsupported claim or produced a defensible paraphrase that the automatic measure undervalued. A score change could then be examined through actual behaviour rather than treated as a self-explanatory improvement.

The Programme Before the Microphone Opened

This original fictional case supplies all evidence needed for the questions.

A

A college radio club prepared an evening programme featuring an interview, student music and notices. The first plan was simply a list of items. During rehearsal, members discovered that knowing the content was not enough to connect it into a clear broadcast. Someone had to identify the current version, manage the time, explain what was recorded and check what could be shared. The producer began a running order and production log. The documents were meant to make responsibilities visible while leaving room for a conversation that could not be scripted word for word.

B

The running order separated scheduled clock time from an item’s duration. An interview expected to last seven minutes was not assigned to seven o’clock merely because both involved the number seven. The team also marked transitions and the time available for them. A sum of recorded clip lengths could otherwise leave out every introduction and pause between items. The producer used the plan to see where a delay would affect later parts, not as proof that a live contribution would end at the exact second originally imagined.

C

A recorded interview did not become live because it was played during a live programme. The introduction identified it as recorded earlier. Words such as today in the clip were checked against the broadcast context, and any necessary explanation was added outside the guest’s original speech. The team did not pretend the guest was currently in the studio. It kept the meaning of the recording and the circumstances of its transmission distinct, so a useful earlier conversation would not mislead listeners about when a statement or event had occurred.

D

The music segment followed the club’s stated permissions and the agreements relevant to each recording. A performer’s willingness to play at a college event was not automatically treated as permission for every later broadcast or online use. The producer checked the proposed uses rather than infer them from possession of an audio file. The log identified the source and the permission record. The point was not to describe every possible legal situation, but to make sure this programme used material within the arrangements the club had actually obtained.

E

The guest’s name was checked directly for the form and pronunciation she wanted used in the programme. A familiar spelling did not guarantee the presenter’s first attempt was right. The note was a production aid, not a public display of the guest’s private contact information. The presenter also checked the job title that would appear in the introduction. A person could help confirm those facts without being given authority to rewrite unrelated editorial choices. The record named which details had been checked and by whom.

F

Room sound affected the interview recording. A periodic click from nearby equipment could be more noticeable in a quiet answer than in a loud group discussion. The team listened to the actual recording before deciding what treatment was appropriate. It did not assume that a silent room photograph proved the microphone had captured no background sound. Any edited version remained linked to the original, with a note about the change. This helped the producer distinguish a deliberate pause in the conversation from a gap or noise introduced during recording and editing.

G

Clip levels required more than comparing the single highest peak. Two excerpts could reach a similar maximum while one sounded much louder through most of its length. The producer checked the programme’s stated playback conditions and adjusted within the approved process. Raising every quiet section as far as possible could also change the intended impression. The aim was a usable relationship among the programme’s parts, not a contest in which the loudest file won. The log recorded which prepared version was selected for transmission.

H

The transcript supported reading access and later searching, but it did not silently replace the recording. The team identified whether it followed the spoken wording closely or had been edited for readability. Removing a repeated start could help a reader while changing the visible rhythm of an answer. The transcript was dated and connected to the relevant audio version. This allowed a listener or reader to understand why the words on the page might differ slightly from an earlier clip rather than assume that every discrepancy was necessarily an error by the guest.

I

The team rehearsed a technical interruption. A named presenter would use a prepared short explanation while the producer dealt with the problem. Several members were not expected to speak different instructions at once. The rehearsal tested who acted and how the programme returned to the running order. It did not prove that every possible failure had been predicted. The club wanted a bounded response it understood, with a way to record what happened, rather than trust that someone would improvise a clear transition simply because the microphones were available.

J

Listeners could send messages during the show. Receipt of a message did not automatically mean its full contents and sender details could be read aloud. The club’s submission notice and production process explained the intended uses. A useful question might be shortened or presented without unnecessary identifying detail. The producer distinguished private contact information from the contribution selected for broadcast. Audience participation became clearer when people could understand that boundary, rather than discover only after transmission that a message meant for the club had become a public statement.

K

The later online edition included its release date and notes about time-sensitive notices. A clip inviting listeners to an event that had already happened was not left to sound like a current invitation. The team could remove or contextualise that part under its editing policy while preserving a record of the original live programme. The broadcast and the later edition served different situations. A successful live evening was therefore not the final production task; the account of what a later listener would hear also required attention.

This original fictional case supplies all evidence needed for the questions.

A

A college garden club compared two seed varieties for its public growing display. Members hoped to name a winner at the end of term. Their tutor first asked what winner would mean: the quickest early growth, the largest harvest or the most dependable result under limited care. The club wrote down its questions before planting. It wanted a useful record for future gardeners, rather than an attractive poster that turned every visible difference into proof that one packet was simply better than the other.

B

Seed packets carried identifiers for the variety and the purchased batch. The club kept both. Two packets with the same variety name could have different storage histories, while a supplier’s batch number did not automatically explain every difference between the plants. The record linked the material used to the place it was planted. Members did not replace those identifiers with informal names such as the good packet after seeing results. The labels needed to support later checking, including the possibility that the first impression would change.

C

The number planted and the number observed growing were recorded separately. A plot containing more seedlings could simply have received more seeds. The club compared relevant proportions and stated the counting date. A percentage also needed its starting number visible: a result based on a few seeds could be less informative about variation than the same percentage from a larger set. The tutor did not reject every small observation. She made sure the size and meaning of the observation travelled with the number printed on the chart.

D

Planting date, depth and the agreed care routine were recorded. If one group was planted earlier, its extra growth time could matter to a later height comparison. Members followed the club’s supervised plan and noted departures from it. They did not assume that writing one common instruction meant it had been carried out identically everywhere. The record included what had actually happened as far as the club could establish. A plan was useful for coordination, while observations were needed to interpret whether the intended comparison had been achieved.

E

The first suggested layout put one variety along the sunny edge and the other near a shaded wall. The tutor explained that variety and position would then be mixed together in the result. The club used its stated assignment plan to distribute varieties across the available areas and recorded the map. This reduced one avoidable problem without guaranteeing that every small environmental difference disappeared. The point was to make the arrangement and its remaining limits visible, rather than trust that a neat pair of rows automatically formed a fair comparison.

F

Several appropriately assigned plots gave information about variation. Copying one plot’s label onto several photographs did not create several independent trials. The club also distinguished repeated observations of the same plants from observations of additional plots. Both could be useful, but they answered different questions. The record preserved plot identity through the term, so a later chart would not count every visit as a new set of plants. The tutor wanted members to understand what had been repeated before announcing that a result had been repeated many times.

G

Height was measured under a stated method at named times. A plant measured to the tip of its tallest leaf could appear different from one measured to a different point. The club agreed on the relevant feature and noted exceptions. It also kept early growth records separate from later harvest results. A fast start did not establish the largest final output. Members could describe the time course rather than select only the date on which their preferred variety looked most impressive and call that the whole experiment.

H

Harvest weight needed a preparation description. Fresh material with water on it could not automatically be compared with material prepared differently. The club recorded the agreed state and unit, and kept any alternative measure clearly labelled. A number without that information could look exact while combining unlike things. The record did not make weight the only useful outcome. It made this particular quantity interpretable, so someone interested in another property could understand what the chart did and did not show.

The club recorded what was known about the damage and which observations remained usable. It did not automatically remove every inconvenient plot either. The reason for a missing or excluded result mattered to the interpretation. The final table showed the status of the case, allowing a reader to distinguish an observed poor outcome from an observation the planned trial could no longer supply.

The Specimen That Fixed a Name

This original fictional case supplies all evidence needed for the questions.

A

A fictional natural-history museum prepared an exhibition about changing species names. Visitors often assumed that the specimen displayed beneath a name was the best or most typical example of the whole species. The curator began with a different question: what role did this particular object play in the history of the name? Some specimens were important because they had been designated as reference material under the relevant naming rules. Their role connected a name with material evidence; it did not make every aspect of their appearance a definition that all living individuals had to match.

B

A name-bearing type served as an anchor for applying a scientific name. It was not necessarily an average individual or the largest, most complete example in the collection. A single reference object could have unusual features within the broader group. The museum explained this distinction before showing visitors differences among specimens. The point of a fixed reference was to make the use of a name examinable when interpretations changed, not to claim that variation in nature had disappeared or that every individual could be identified from a simple resemblance to one body.

C

Classification and naming were related but not identical activities. A researcher could propose that a group previously treated as one species contained two, or that two named groups should be joined. The role of the name-bearing material helped determine how existing names applied under that proposal. It did not by itself prove the proposal biologically correct. The exhibition separated the hypothesis about relationships and boundaries from the rules used to connect names to the recognised groups, so a name change would not be mistaken for a discovery produced by a label alone.

D

Early descriptions recorded the features their authors considered useful and could observe. Failure to mention a feature did not automatically mean the original specimen lacked it. A later method might reveal a detail the first account did not examine. The Water Arrived at Different Times

This original fictional case supplies all evidence needed for the questions.

A

A fictional district proposed several small projects to reduce pressure on a river during heavy rain. Each village could describe a useful local measure, but the catchment team asked how the measures interacted. Water stored in one place, delayed in another or redirected through a channel could affect people beyond the project boundary. The report followed the connected system rather than assume that several individually attractive diagrams would add up to one self-explanatory regional solution. It documented timing, location and the objectives under which the proposals were compared.

B

The catchment was defined by relevant drainage relationships and documented engineered connections, not simply the lines separating local councils. A project inside one administrative area could influence flow in another. The team mapped those relationships before assigning responsibilities. It did not conclude that political boundaries were irrelevant to decisions; they mattered to authority and funding. They were not, however, a substitute for the physical and managed routes through which water moved. The report kept the two kinds of boundary visible so an institutional map would not silently become a hydrological model.

C

The same rainfall total could produce different runoff under different conditions. Soil state, surface cover and the sequence of earlier rain could affect how much water entered a channel and how quickly. The team recorded these assumptions rather than treat a rainfall number as the complete description of an event. A model could be useful while conditional. Its results were attached to the scenario used, not presented as if every storm with an equal total would create an identical response across every part of the district.

D

A storage area’s water level was not the same quantity as stored volume or available capacity. Shape mattered: the same vertical change could correspond to different amounts in different basins. The team used the appropriate relationship for each proposed site. A photograph of a low level did not automatically show more empty storage than another site’s higher mark. The report labelled the quantities and units. This prevented a comparison of unlike shapes from appearing precise merely because every diagram had used the same number of centimetres on its vertical scale.

E

Timing among tributaries mattered as well as total volume. Delaying one inflow could reduce a peak in one scenario, but in another it could make that inflow coincide more closely with a different tributary’s peak. The team therefore examined the arrival pattern downstream. It did not treat delay as automatically beneficial at every location and under every sequence. The proposed measure had to be considered within a connected event, where shifting a process in time could change its interaction with processes that another project did not control.

F

A local benefit could be accompanied by consequences elsewhere. Protecting a village’s immediate site did not by itself establish an overall gain for all places affected. The team described where water or risk might be redistributed and under which assumptions. It did not use this possibility to reject every local project. It required the comparison to include the relevant wider area and the people affected. An attractive result drawn at one boundary was not the end of the evaluation simply because the organisation commissioning the drawing operated within that boundary.

G

Forecasts informed preparation but did not provide a timetable guaranteed to occur. The team considered a range of stated scenarios and explained the uncertainty in rainfall and response. A precise-looking predicted time could be useful without becoming certain to the minute. The report distinguished a current forecast, a modelled scenario and a later observation. These records could be compared after an event, but the comparison should not pretend that the information available afterwards had already been known when a decision was made.

H

Installed capacity depended on condition and operation. A channel designed to convey a given amount could perform differently if obstructed or if a control did not work as assumed. The project accounts included inspection and maintenance responsibilities rather than report construction as proof of permanent availability. This did not imply that every structure was failing. It connected a claimed capability with the continuing conditions under which it could be relied upon. A successful opening-day demonstration was evidence about that occasion, not an unlimited guarantee across the life of the scheme.

I

Measurements came from particular points and periods. A gauge on one tributary did not record every branch of the river system. The team noted locations, units and the relationship between a reading and the quantity inferred. Flow rate described movement per unit time; it was not itself a total volume over an unnamed period. The record also identified gaps in observation. A clean line in a dashboard could otherwise suggest continuous direct knowledge where the model had filled missing intervals or where no instrument had measured that part of the system.

J

Ecological objectives could concern the pattern of flows rather than only one annual average. Short pulses, low periods and seasonal timing could matter differently to a habitat. The team considered these relationships where they were relevant to the project’s stated scope. It did not assume that maintaining a constant line at an average value would reproduce the ecological conditions of the varying river. The environmental account remained connected to what organisms and habitats experienced over time, instead of reduce every objective to the same summary used for a construction estimate.

K

Residents and land managers supplied observations about local changes, blocked routes and past events. The team checked them with other evidence and recorded their sources. A person’s experience could reveal something the model had missed without making every recollection exact. Conversely, numerical output did not become decisive merely because it was produced by software. The process provided a route for a well-supported correction and retained unresolved disagreement where necessary. Local knowledge and instruments were treated as different contributions to a shared question, not rivals from which one had to win in every case.

L

The distribution of effects mattered to the policy decision. A small aggregate improvement could conceal a worse outcome for a particular group, and people could disagree about the trade-off. The report showed where gains, costs and remaining risks fell rather than hide them inside one net number. Measurement could inform the discussion but could not silently choose what distribution was acceptable. The decision record named the objective and who had participated, allowing an observer to distinguish a technical estimate from the judgement made using it.

M

A rehearsal tested coordination under a constructed scenario. Staff practised who would receive information, make a decision and explain a change to others. Passing the exercise showed something about that process under its designed conditions. It did not prove every real event would unfold the same way. The team kept the scenario, actions and limitations together in the record. This allowed a later exercise to test a different weakness rather than repeat a reassuring script and count each repetition as independent evidence of universal readiness.

N

Model versions were linked to the observations and assumptions used. Updating a parameter could change a diagram without any physical alteration to the river. The team retained earlier outputs with their status instead of leave only a current picture under an unchanged label. A later reviewer could investigate whether a difference came from new evidence, a revised interpretation or a real change at the site. The report did not ask every reader to rerun the model, but it provided a traceable account of how the result had been produced.

O

The final proposal described expected effects within scenarios and the monitoring needed after work. It did not offer an unconditional promise that water would always arrive in a manageable way. Its practical value lay in clarifying what each measure addressed, how it interacted with the catchment and what would trigger reconsideration. The district could make a decision without claiming that uncertainty had vanished. The account remained open to later evidence, so the connected system was not reduced to the boundaries of the last diagram printed for a meeting.

The final proposal described expected effects within scenarios and the monitoring needed after work. It did not offer an unconditional promise that water would always arrive in a manageable way. Its practical value lay in clarifying what each measure addressed, how it interacted with the catchment and what would trigger reconsideration. The district could make a decision without claiming that uncertainty had vanished. The account remained open to later evidence, so the connected system was not reduced to the boundaries of the last diagram printed for a meeting.
